claim: State can be a JSON object or array containing related context, examples, and other information that helps the model answer the questions.
quote: State can also be a JSON object or array containing related context, examples, and other information that helps the model answer the associated questions.
why: Confirms gather.py may pass structured JSON state rather than one flat string.

claim: TypeSafe recommends using an object for most requests so each part of the state has a descriptive name.
quote: Use an object for most requests so each part of the state has a descriptive name and its relationships remain clear.
why: Directly answers state format and field naming: prefer a named-field object (e.g. claim/quote fields).

claim: All questions in a request see the same state and are evaluated independently.
quote: Each request evaluates one state against one or more questions. All questions see the same state and are evaluated independently.
why: Question independence: per-card criteria can be batched without cross-talk.

claim: Jev 1.13's context length is 64k tokens per request and 32k tokens for state plus the longest question.
quote: 64k tokens per request; 32k tokens for `state` plus the longest question
why: Hard cap on how much card/page text can go in state.

claim: For jev-1.13, accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision, which acts as a distractor.
quote: Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision. Unrelated detail acts as a distractor, and a large state makes it harder to tell which part of the input produced a wrong answer.
why: Context rot: trim state to only the card fields needed. Date is the page's 'Last reviewed' date.

claim: In TypeSafe's Choice confidence formula only the top probability counts, so (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) and (0.6, 0.2, 0.2) both have confidence 0.4.
quote: Only the top probability counts, so $(0.6, 0.3, 0.1)$ and $(0.6, 0.2, 0.2)$ both have confidence 0.4.
why: Choice confidence ignores runner-up spread; docs suggest top-to-second ratio as an alternative if that matters.

claim: Under TypeSafe's Score confidence formula with three levels, (0, 0.5, 0.5) has confidence 0.25 and (0.5, 0, 0.5) has confidence 0.
quote: With three levels, $(0, 0.5, 0.5)$ has confidence 0.25, because the model is torn between two adjacent levels. $(0.5, 0, 0.5)$ has confidence 0, because it is torn between opposite ends.
why: Score confidence is distance-aware, unlike Choice; relevant to choosing Score for ordered relevance levels.

claim: TypeSafe returns no separate confidence for a Noul answer, whose single probability p already carries the uncertainty.
quote: A Noul answer is a single probability $p$ that the answer is yes, and TypeSafe returns no separate `confidence` for it. The probability already carries the uncertainty
why: gather.py must derive a gate from p (docs suggest |2p-1|) for Noul questions.

claim: TypeSafe describes a fractional Score as a position that can be used to rank or rounded to the nearest level.
quote: A fractional score is a position. You can use it to rank reports by severity, or round it to the nearest level when your code needs one outcome.
why: Score fractional values; page also says the score is a probability-weighted mean of level numbers.

claim: In TypeSafe's parallel-questions cookbook, most answers came back identical across all 5 repeats with std dev exactly 0.0, whether batched or not.
quote: Most answers came back identical across all 5 repeats either way, the same value on every call, std dev exactly 0.0.
why: Determinism evidence: largely deterministic, though the same page notes two nouls had small run-to-run noise.

claim: In the cookbook, there was no batching effect: no question's answer depended on the 12 other questions sharing its request.
quote: Either way, there is no batching effect: no question's answer depends on the 12 other questions sharing its request.
why: Empirical support that batching all card questions in one call is safe and cheaper.

claim: jev-1.13 does not count reliably, including characters in a word, occurrences of a term in a passage, and items in a long list.
quote: `jev-1.13` does not count reliably. This covers characters in a word, occurrences of a term in a passage, and items in a long list.
why: Limits: counting must stay in code.

claim: jev-1.13 reads dates as text, so asking which of two dates comes first, how far apart they are, or whether one is inside a window is unreliable.
quote: `jev-1.13` reads dates as text, not as ordered quantities. Asking which of two dates comes first, how far apart they are, or whether one falls inside a window is unreliable.
why: Recency/date checks on cards (published field) should be computed in code.

claim: English is Jev's primary training language with the best accuracy, while other languages including CJK scripts are handled but not equally well.
quote: English is the primary training language and where accuracy is currently best. Other languages, including CJK scripts, are handled but not equally well
why: Language support limit for non-English evidence.

claim: Lindfors measured Jev's tokenizer at about 2.06 characters per token on Norwegian, making the 32k-token state limit roughly 64,000 characters.
quote: Jev's tokenizer gets about 2.06 characters per token on Norwegian. The limit for the state is 32k tokens, so that is roughly 64,000 characters of Norwegian
why: Independent context-cap measurement; non-English text consumes the cap faster.

claim: JevAdvBench found that on jev-1.13.0 one unverified opinion appended to the state flips 12.1% of decisions, statistically tied with the strongest injected command (10.1%).
quote: In contrast, one unverified opinion appended to the state flips 12.1% of decisions, statistically tied with the strongest injected command (10.1%)
why: State content (e.g. opinionated page text in quotes) can move decisions; arXiv preprint, not formally peer reviewed.
